1.title: Leading Teams: Leadership, Conflict and Knowledge
1.text: Welcome to Module 5. This module is the second of the People domain modules, and it is about the team itself. In Part 1, we look at leading the team: expectations, leadership style, empowerment and problem solving. Part 2 covers people, motivation and conflict. Part 3 covers knowledge: how to find it, capture it and transfer it. Throughout, the best answers tend to talk to the people involved first.

1.title: Where This Module Sits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits. The People domain carries about a third of the exam. This module covers three of its eight tasks. Task three: lead the project team. Task two: manage conflicts. Task seven: help ensure knowledge transfer. They map to our three parts. The habit that pays off across all three: talk to the people involved before analyzing documents, escalating or imposing a fix.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Set team-level expectations, a team charter and the right leadership style. Empower the team, solve problems and represent the team's voice. Support varied perspectives, motivate people and clarify roles. Run the conflict process: source, context, technique, agreement and escalation. Set and enforce ground rules. And identify, capture and transfer critical knowledge.

1.title: Case Check-In: Two Teams, One Goal
1.text: In our case, two teams must work together. The controller engineers are formal and hardware-minded, and they want the interface frozen early. The dashboard developers are agile and iterative, and they want the interface to adapt each iteration. Both share one goal: a reliable microgrid with a trustworthy dashboard. You are the project manager and servant leader. Over this module you will set expectations, choose a leadership style, manage the conflict and protect critical knowledge.

1.title: Key Terms
1.text: Six terms. Lead the team means improving competencies, interactions and the team environment to raise performance. Servant leadership means serving the needs and development of team members to enable the highest performance. Management can be centralized, with authority and accountability held by one person, or distributed, with authority spread across empowered teams. The team charter holds the team's values, communication guidelines, decision and conflict rules, and agreements. Emotional intelligence is the ability to identify and manage your own and others' emotions. And empowerment is authority over how work is done, within boundaries.

1.title: Management Versus Leadership
1.text: Management and leadership are different. Management activities focus on the means of meeting objectives: effective processes, planning, coordinating, measuring and monitoring. Leadership activities focus on people: influencing, motivating, listening and enabling. Leadership is the knowledge, skills and behaviors needed to guide, motivate and direct a team to achieve business goals. It includes negotiation, resilience, communication, problem solving, critical thinking and interpersonal skills. It is useful to all members, whether authority is centralized or shared. You need both management and leadership.

1.title: Seven Enablers of Leading the Team
1.text: The ECO lists seven enablers for leading the project team. Establish expectations at the team level. Determine an appropriate leadership style. Empower the team. Solve problems. Represent the voice of the team. Support varied experiences, skills and perspectives. And establish clear roles and responsibilities. We take the first five in this part, and the last two, along with motivation, at the start of Part 2.

1.title: Establish Expectations at the Team Level
1.text: Start with expectations at the team level. Communicate the vision and objectives, and use them when the team decides and solves problems. Co-create a team charter and working agreements covering values, communication, decision-making, conflict resolution and meeting rules. Agree ground rules and norms, with a way to handle violations. Set performance and quality expectations, such as the definition of done and acceptance criteria. Hold a deliberate kickoff. And give guidance and growth: goals for improvement and support for individual development. Revisit the charter when new members join.

1.title: Stages of Team Development
1.text: Teams develop through stages: forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning. The leadership emphasis changes with them. A new team needs structure and direction: vision, roles, expectations and ground rules. A team storming over approach needs coaching and facilitation: surface issues and reinforce agreements. A norming team needs support. A performing team needs delegation and servant leadership: remove impediments and protect the team. At adjourning, recognize and release. In a crisis, be directive briefly, then return to your normal style.

1.title: Choosing a Leadership Style
1.text: How do you choose a style? Weigh the team: its maturity, stage, competence and willingness. Weigh the task: its complexity, urgency and risk. Weigh the organization: its culture and governance, centralized or distributed. Weigh the development approach and where the team sits. And weigh how new the work is to the organization: new work calls for more oversight and a more direct style, while experienced teams are more self-managing. No style fits every moment.

1.title: Style by Situation
1.text: Here is a quick guide. A newly formed team with unclear roles needs directing and structure. A conflict over approach needs coaching and facilitation. A maturing team needs support and delegation. A high-performing, experienced team needs servant leadership and empowerment. A crisis, a safety issue or a compliance deadline calls for a directive style for the moment, then return to your normal style and review. And in a matrix environment with little authority, rely on influence: persuade, listen, and build mutual trust.

1.title: Situational Leadership
1.text: PMBOK 8 names situational leadership. The four-style model is exam practice. Choose the style from the person's competence and commitment for that task. A low-competence, high-commitment beginner needs directing: tell, show and check closely. Someone with some competence and dropping commitment needs coaching: explain, ask questions, encourage. Someone with high competence and variable confidence needs support: listen, praise and share the decision. Someone with high competence and high commitment gets delegation: agree the outcome and leave the how to them.

1.title: Styles and the Risk of Overuse
1.text: Every style has a strength and a risk when overused. Servant leadership clears the way, but decisions can drift when the team needs a firm call. Transactional leadership gives clear rewards, but people do only what is rewarded. Transformational leadership inspires commitment, but constant stretch exhausts people. Laissez-faire gives maximum autonomy, but goals blur. Directive leadership gives speed in a crisis, but breeds resentment. Participative leadership builds buy-in, but decisions slow down. PMBOK 8 pairs Theory X with hands-on leadership, Theory Y with coaching, and servant leadership with self-managing teams.

1.title: Empower the Team
1.text: Empower the team. Delegate decisions about how the work is done and about the details of deliverables, within clear boundaries: decision rights, guardrails and escalation points. Create the conditions: trust, clear purpose, skills, information and safety to speak. Stay available: coach, remove barriers and protect the team, but do not abdicate. Escalate decisions beyond the team's authority, with analysis and a recommendation. Two signals to read correctly. Healthy metrics with falling morale: meet the team first. A mature team whose tasks are still assigned by the project manager: let the team distribute its daily work.

1.title: Solve Problems
1.text: PMBOK 8 gives a structured approach to problem solving. Define the problem. Identify the root cause. Generate possible solutions. Choose the best. Implement it. And verify effectiveness. Useful tools include critical thinking, which questions assumptions and spots bias. Also root cause analysis and Six Thinking Hats. Decision-making methods that diverge and then converge limit groupthink. And retrospectives help too. As a leader, facilitate rather than solve everything yourself, and escalate beyond your authority with alternatives.

1.title: Represent the Voice of the Team
1.text: Represent the voice of the team. Speak for the team to the sponsor, governance and stakeholders: capacity limits, impediments, risks, needs and achievements. Protect the team by routing new requests through the backlog or change process, and by showing trade-offs and capacity data. Bring insight upward and decisions downward, transparently, and share credit. Do not speak for the team without its input, and do not filter its concerns. Remove the impediments that the team cannot remove itself.

1.title: Leadership in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
1.text: Leadership looks different by approach. In predictive work, leadership is centralized: the project manager directs and coordinates, and roles come from the responsibility matrix. In agile work, leadership is distributed and servant, and the team self-organizes. The product owner, team and facilitator hold the roles. Decisions: escalation chains in predictive work, the team decides how and the product owner decides priority in agile work. Improvement comes at gates, or in a retrospective every iteration. Hybrid is centralized for the envelope and distributed inside iterations.

1.title: Leadership Traps: What PMI Expects
1.text: The traps for Part 1. Match the style to the stage and situation, and use a directive style only briefly in a crisis. Do not impose a decision to end a storming debate. Facilitate and reinforce the team's agreements. Empower within boundaries: do not micromanage, and do not abdicate. Represent the team's voice and protect its capacity when it asks you to. Adapt the process to people, for example by accepting written input, rather than forcing people to change. And make authority match responsibility. Healthy metrics can hide disengagement, so meet the team first.

1.title: Part 1 Recap
1.text: Let us recap Part 1. Set expectations with a vision, a charter, ground rules and a kickoff. Choose the style by stage and situation, and be directive only briefly in a crisis. Situational leadership looks at competence and commitment for the task. Empower the team with decision rights within boundaries. Solve problems by defining, finding the root cause, generating options, choosing, implementing and verifying. And represent the team's voice: protect its capacity, and do not filter its concerns. In Part 2, we look at people, motivation and conflict.

2.title: Support Varied Experiences, Skills and Perspectives
2.text: Part 2 begins with people. Create a safe, respectful and nonjudgmental environment, and welcome disagreement as dialogue rather than debate. Adapt to people: written or asynchronous input suits members who are quiet in meetings but strong in writing. Mix seniority and expertise to create coaching and mentoring. Coaching asks questions to help a person find a solution, while mentoring is long-term guidance by sharing experience. Use cultural intelligence without stereotyping. Be open about bias. And watch workload and signs of burnout.

2.title: Emotional Intelligence
2.text: Emotional intelligence has four areas. Self-awareness: a realistic self-assessment. Self-management: thinking before acting. Social awareness: empathy and reading cues. Social skills: building rapport, building teams and finding common ground. Emotional intelligence is the basis of all forms of leadership, and emotionally competent teams are more effective, with less turnover. Use skill matrices and individual and team assessments, such as surveys, interviews and focus groups, to understand strengths and preferences.

2.title: Clear Roles and Responsibilities
2.text: Establish clear roles and responsibilities. A role is a function. A responsibility is a duty. Authority is the right to decide, approve and apply resources. And competence is skill and capacity. Authority should match responsibility. Use a responsibility assignment matrix, such as a RACI chart, with one accountable owner per activity. Fill competence gaps through training, coaching, mentoring or reassignment. In agile teams, titles vary and the functions matter. With vendors, clarify who directs whose people and the reporting lines. Revisit roles when people join, leave or change.

2.title: Motivation Theories
2.text: Motivation theories appear in scenarios as cues. Maslow: needs run from basic to self-actualization, and a satisfied need stops motivating. Herzberg: hygiene factors such as pay and conditions prevent dissatisfaction, while motivators such as achievement and recognition create satisfaction. McClelland: needs for achievement, power and affiliation. McGregor: Theory X assumes people avoid work, Theory Y assumes they seek responsibility, Theory Z adds long-term commitment. Pink: autonomy, mastery and purpose. Vroom, as exam practice: people are motivated when effort leads to performance, and performance to a valued reward.

2.title: Recognition, Rewards and Team Building
2.text: Recognition and rewards: understand what motivates each person, because cultural differences change what is meaningful. Money is tangible, but intangible rewards can be as effective or more. Most members are motivated by growth, accomplishment, appreciation and applying their skills. Recognize throughout the project, not only at the end, and celebrate quick wins. Team building is a continuous process, from a five-minute agenda item to an off-site event, and it is valuable for remote teams. Training can be formal or informal.

2.title: High-Performing Teams
2.text: High-performing teams show open communication, shared understanding and shared ownership. They show trust and collaboration. They show adaptability and resilience. And they show empowerment and autonomy, and recognition. Leaders role-model transparency, integrity, respect, positive discourse, support, courage and celebrating success. Team performance assessment, formal or informal, looks at indicators such as improved skills, lower turnover and greater cohesion. Use the findings to choose training, coaching or other changes. For virtual teams, try to hold at least one face-to-face meeting.

2.title: Conflict: What It Is
2.text: Now conflict. Conflict is inevitable in a project environment. Sources include scarce resources, scheduling priorities and personal work styles. Managed well, differences of opinion can increase creativity and improve decisions. PMBOK 8's core rules: address conflict early, usually in private, with a direct and collaborative approach. Team members are initially responsible for resolving a conflict that becomes negative. If it escalates, the project manager helps facilitate. If disruptive conflict continues, formal procedures may be used, including disciplinary action.

2.title: Managing a Conflict Step by Step
2.text: The conflict process has six steps. One, identify the source. Two, analyze the context. Three, choose a technique that fits. Four, run the resolution in a safe space, focusing on issues, not people. Five, agree and document who will do what. Six, follow up to check that it holds. Escalate in steps if it does not. Notice that choosing a technique comes third. Many wrong answers jump straight to a technique, a punishment or an escalation before finding the source.

2.title: Sources of Conflict
2.text: Know the common sources. Scarce resources: two teams competing for the same specialist or budget. Scheduling priorities. Personal work styles. Roles and accountability: two parties believe they own the work, or nobody does. Requirements and expectations, even from the same signed document. Incentives and objectives that reward opposing behaviors, such as speed against thoroughness. And communication, culture and change, including an informal change nobody recorded. With personality clashes, address behavior and the work, not the person.

2.title: Find the Real Source
2.text: The argument you see is rarely the cause. Under the surface may be an undefined handoff, an informal change that nobody recorded, a gap in accountability where no single owner exists, or incentives that reward opposing behavior. Trace the dispute back to its origin, then fix the cause, not only the symptom. If opposing incentives drive repeated clashes, work with the managers who set them to align objectives. And if both parties signed the same document and still disagree, facilitate a discussion. Rereading the text will not settle it.

2.title: Analyze the Context
2.text: Analyze the context before choosing a technique. PMBOK 8 lists five factors. The importance and intensity of the conflict. The time pressure for resolving it. The relative power of the people involved. The importance of maintaining a good relationship. And the motivation to resolve it, in the short or long term. In addition, consider who is involved, and whether both positions are sound. Consider whether there is a safety, compliance or ethics element. And consider whether the cause is structural or personal.

2.title: Five Resolution Techniques
2.text: Five techniques. Collaborate, also called problem-solve, incorporates multiple viewpoints and gives consensus and commitment: win-win. Compromise searches for solutions that give some satisfaction to all parties, and is occasionally lose-lose. Force, or direct, pushes one viewpoint, and is win-lose. Smooth, or accommodate, emphasizes agreement to preserve the relationship. Withdraw, or avoid, retreats from or postpones the conflict. PMBOK 8 says each has its place. The typical-use guidance is exam practice: collaborate when time and importance allow, and force only for emergencies or safety.

2.title: Running the Resolution
2.text: How do you run the resolution? Create a safe space, and keep communication open and respectful in words, tone and body language. Focus on the issues, not the people, because conflict arises when people perceive situations differently. Focus on the present and future, not the past. Search for alternatives together, moving the conflict into a problem-solving space. Facilitate an agreement, document who will do what, and follow up. And escalate in steps when needed. When two directors expect different dates, hold a joint session to agree one.

2.title: Case Check-In: The Interface Conflict
2.text: Back to our case. The engineers want the interface frozen. The developers want it adapted each iteration. First, find the source. Here, an informal interface change was never recorded, so each team believes it is right. Second, facilitate a joint session, focusing on issues, not people, on the present and future, and on alternatives together. Third, agree one rule: baseline interface changes go to the change board, and feature changes go to the product owner. Then document it and follow up.

2.title: Escalating in Steps
2.text: Escalate in steps. First, the parties involved try to resolve it. Second, the project manager facilitates a satisfactory resolution. Third, management or the sponsor steps in, for example when objectives and incentives are beyond your authority. Fourth, formal procedures, including disciplinary action, if disruptive conflict continues. Ethics or compliance violations follow organizational policy and the PMI Code of Ethics. A common wrong answer jumps to the last step, or to escalation before the parties have tried.

2.title: Ground Rules and Conflict Principles
2.text: Communicate the conflict principles early. Tell people the rules of the game: how disagreements are raised and resolved, who facilitates, and when matters escalate. Put them in the team charter, the communications plan and, for vendors and partners, in the agreements, including dispute resolution clauses. State the four principles: open and respectful communication, issues not people, present and future, and alternatives together. Include external stakeholders at kickoff. Model the behavior. And prevent conflict with ground rules, role definition, clear priorities and shared objectives.

2.title: Ground Rules That Stick
2.text: Ground rules stick when the team owns them. Create them together: the charter works best when the team develops it. Communicate them to everyone, including new members, who should help shape the rules rather than be handed them privately. Reinforce them consistently: leaders follow them first, adherence is recognized, and they apply to everyone. And respond to breaches early and privately. Revisit them when new members join and when the context changes, such as virtual working or a new vendor. Make it safe to speak up.

2.title: Rectifying Ground Rule Violations
2.text: When a ground rule is violated, follow these steps. Notice early, and address small breaches before they grow. Talk privately, stating facts, listening to the reason, and not assuming motives. Refer to the agreement the team created. If the charter is the team's, involve the team: facilitate a team discussion on honoring it, rather than enforcing individually or imposing a new process. Coach and follow up. Fix the system if the rule is unclear or unworkable. And use formal routes for repeated or serious breaches. Ethics violations follow the Code.

2.title: Conflict in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
2.text: Conflict handling differs by approach. In predictive work, the team charter and organizational policy set the ground rules, and the project manager enforces them within authority. The parties come first, then the project manager and functional managers. Priority conflicts go to change control and sponsor decisions. In agile work, working agreements belong to the team, the team responds first with the servant leader facilitating, and the product owner orders the backlog for priority conflicts. Forums are daily coordination meetings and retrospectives. Hybrid combines both.

2.title: Conflict Traps: What PMI Expects
2.text: The traps for conflict. Find the source first. Collaborate when time allows, compromise when time is short, force only for emergencies, and avoid or smooth only for minor issues. Address conflict early, privately and directly. Team members try first, the project manager facilitates, and formal procedures come last. Focus on issues, not people, and on the present and future. Align objectives when incentives conflict. A team-made charter is enforced by the team. And new members help shape the ground rules.

2.title: Part 2 Recap
2.text: Let us recap Part 2. For people: include everyone, build emotional intelligence, and clarify roles with one accountable owner. Motivate with growth, autonomy and purpose, and recognize early and often. The conflict process runs source, context, technique, resolution, agreement and follow-up. The five techniques are collaborate, compromise, force, smooth and withdraw. Escalate from the parties, to the project manager, to management, to formal procedures. And ground rules are co-created, communicated, reinforced and enforced by the team. In Part 3, we turn to knowledge.

3.title: Knowledge: Why It Matters
3.text: Part 3 covers knowledge. Manage Project Knowledge means using existing knowledge and creating new knowledge to achieve project objectives and contribute to organizational learning. It is more than documenting, or collecting lessons at the end. Knowledge management connects people, to create and share knowledge. Information management connects people to information. Lessons learned show how events were or should be addressed to improve future performance. And critical knowledge held by one person is a risk. Capture it from people before they leave.

3.title: Explicit and Tacit Knowledge
3.text: Two kinds of knowledge. Explicit knowledge is formal and codifiable in words, pictures or numbers, and is easy to communicate, such as manuals and procedures. It lacks context and can be misread. Tacit knowledge is embedded in a person's mind: skills, insight and practical judgment. It has context but is hard to articulate and transfer. Share tacit knowledge through a collaborative, trust-filled environment: conversation, mentoring, team building, face-to-face interaction and brainstorming. Convert tacit to explicit when possible, but expect judgment to be shared by interaction.

3.title: How Knowledge Changes Form
3.text: As exam practice, four modes describe how knowledge changes form. Socialization: tacit to tacit, like a new analyst shadowing a veteran. Externalization: tacit to explicit, like a retiring engineer's troubleshooting rules written up as a checklist. Combination: explicit to explicit, like three test reports compiled into one summary. Internalization: explicit to tacit, like a new hire running a documented procedure until it becomes second nature. To name the mode, look at the starting form and the ending form.

3.title: The Manage Project Knowledge Process
3.text: Here is the process. The benefit is to use earlier knowledge and collect new knowledge to support operations and future work. Tools include expert judgment, knowledge and information management, after-action reviews, in-progress postmortems, retrospectives, storytelling and interpersonal skills. The main output is the lessons learned register, plus plan updates and process asset updates. Plan how and when lessons will be captured. The people doing the work capture them, in text, audio, video or pictures. AI can be a source, but exposes sensitive data and may hallucinate.

3.title: Identify Knowledge Critical to the Project
3.text: How do you identify critical knowledge? Ask five questions. What must the project, the next phase or operations be able to do that depends on specific know-how? Who holds it? Look for single points of failure such as experts, vendor specialists, retirees and people whose assignment is ending. What would losing it cost? How hard is it to rebuild? Judgment is harder to rebuild than procedures. And what do earlier projects offer? Capture from people first, before they leave, and record knowledge loss as a risk.

3.title: Gather Explicit Knowledge
3.text: Gather explicit knowledge in the lessons learned register. Each entry has a category and a description of the situation, the impacts, the recommendations and the proposed actions. It covers challenges, problems, realized risks and opportunities. Capture continuously, not only at closure. At the end, the register moves to the organization's lessons learned repository. Make records searchable and categorized, with a way to contact the originator. Use information management too: libraries, web search, the project information system and document systems. And walk the next team through the key lessons instead of just sending a log.

3.title: Gather Tacit Knowledge
3.text: Gather tacit knowledge through interaction. After-action reviews ask four questions: what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why were there differences, and what can we learn. Run retrospectives at least every iteration, and in-progress postmortems at stages of the life cycle. Use work shadowing and reverse shadowing, pairing, mentoring, interviews, including AI interview bots, learning-review workshops and brainstorming. Storytelling conveys lessons and good practice in a relatable, memorable way, and is particularly effective for tacit knowledge.

3.title: Foster an Environment for Knowledge Transfer
3.text: Foster an environment where transfer works. Trust and psychological safety: people share mistakes when they will not be punished, so run blameless reviews. Open collaboration: conversations, communities of practice, forums and virtual tools. Time and space: schedule and protect retrospectives, knowledge cafés and seminars. Mentoring and shadowing: pair successors with experts during the work. Hands-on practice: watching is not doing, so receivers should perform the task with support before handover. A usable repository, walked through with the next team. And recognition for sharing and using lessons.

3.title: Applying Knowledge
3.text: Applying knowledge is where it pays off. Pull earlier lessons into the plan. If a previous project's delays had specific causes, such as late permits or commissioning problems, adjust the plan to address those causes rather than adding a generic buffer. Look for patterns: recurring issues point to changes in procedures and checklists. Feed process assets. Hand over with practice and support, and confirm that the receivers can operate the result. Include vendors and contractors, transferring their expertise to the people who will maintain the system.

3.title: Case Check-In: Handover to Campus Facilities
3.text: Our microgrid will be operated by Campus Facilities. The critical knowledge, such as controller commissioning and battery maintenance, sits with vendor specialists. So record the loss of that knowledge as a risk with an owner, and plan the transfer. Pair Facilities staff with the specialists during commissioning, have them perform the tasks with support before handover, and walk them through the lessons in a searchable register. Watching is not doing. Confirm that Facilities can operate the system before the specialists leave.

3.title: Knowledge in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
3.text: Knowledge looks different by approach. In predictive work, lessons come at phase ends and gates, with in-progress postmortems, and final lessons at closure. Transfer uses mentoring, shadowing and handover training, and records go into the lessons register and a formal repository. In agile work, there is a retrospective every iteration and continuous sharing, with pairing, swarming and shared ownership, and lightweight notes. Actions are a few improvements committed to the next backlog. Hybrid combines both.

3.title: Knowledge Traps: What PMI Expects
3.text: The traps for knowledge. Tacit knowledge needs interaction: shadowing, pairing, mentoring and hands-on practice. Capture critical knowledge from people before they leave, and do not start with document reviews. Watching is not doing, so receivers practice before handover. Capture lessons continuously. Lessons must be usable: searchable, categorized, owned, and walked through with the next team. Make knowledge loss a risk. Foster psychological safety. And use AI responsibly: approved tools, no sensitive data exposure, and verified output.

3.title: Module Recap
3.text: Let us recap the whole module. Lead: set expectations, choose the style by situation, empower within boundaries and represent the team's voice. People: include everyone, build emotional intelligence, clarify roles and motivate with growth, autonomy and purpose. Conflict: find the source first, choose among five techniques, escalate in steps, and keep ground rules owned by the team. Knowledge: identify critical knowledge, capture it from people, and have receivers practice before handover. Now it is time to test yourself. Five questions follow. For each one, pause the video, choose your answer, and then listen to the explanation.

3.title: Practice Question 1
3.text: Question one. A newly formed project team has unclear roles and no agreed way of working, and members keep asking the project manager what is expected of them. Which approach fits best? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. A new team needs structure and direction, so the project manager sets the vision, clarifies roles and agrees ground rules and expectations. Delegating everything, waiting for conflict, or voting on every method leaves the team without the structure it is asking for.

3.title: Practice Question 2
3.text: Question two. Two leads keep arguing about who owns testing of the controller interface. The responsibility matrix lists both as responsible and nobody as accountable. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. The argument is a symptom of a missing accountable owner, so the project manager fixes the cause by clarifying roles and naming one accountable owner. Escalating, leaving it to the leads, or splitting the work leaves the cause in place.

3.title: Practice Question 3
3.text: Question three. A team wrote its own charter, which says that decisions are made in the daily coordination meeting. One member keeps making decisions alone. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. A charter the team created is best enforced by the team, with the project manager facilitating a discussion about honoring the agreement. Warnings, new imposed rules, or a private lecture bypass the team's ownership of its own agreement.

3.title: Practice Question 4
3.text: Question four. A senior engineer who alone knows how to troubleshoot the battery controller will retire in six weeks. What should the project manager do first? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. Tacit know-how is captured from people before they leave, through shadowing, interviews and pairing, with hands-on practice for the successor. A manual alone loses the judgment, a risk entry without action loses the window, and ordering a replacement skips the transfer.

3.title: Practice Question 5
3.text: Question five. The operations team that received the last project's deliverables says its 300-page lessons log was never useful. What is the best way to help the next team? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. Lessons must be usable: searchable, categorized and owned, with a walk-through that connects the next team to the key lessons. More detail, a mandatory read, or a single closing summary do not fix access and interaction.

3.title: Answers at a Glance
3.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: B. A new team needs vision, roles and ground rules. Question two: A. The cause is a missing accountable owner, so assign one. Question three: C. A team-made charter is enforced by the team, with you facilitating. Question four: D. Capture tacit knowledge from the person now, by shadowing and pairing. Question five: A. Make lessons findable and walk the next team through them. That completes Module 5. Next, Module 6 covers business cases, charters, benefits and integrated planning. See you there.
